lessonRef.subject: mathematics
lessonRef.title: Publication, presentation, or reflection: interpreting conditional probability in context

sections.title: Instructional examples
sections.directions: Notice how the explanation names the reason for each step.

items.prompt: 30 people; 18 do A, 14 do B, 7 do both. Find P(A or B).

sections.title: Independent practice
sections.directions: Work on your own. Show the steps that produced each answer.

items.prompt: An event has probability 5/8 on a single trial. Two independent trials are run. Find the probability of at least one success, as a fraction in lowest terms.
A survey table records: group X with 25 successes and 13 failures; group Y with 13 successes and 11 failures. Find P(success | group X) as a fraction in lowest terms.
Two events have P(A) = 6/10, P(B) = 8/10, and P(A and B) = 48/100. Are A and B independent?
choices: No; P(A and B) differs from P(A)·P(B).
No; the two events are mutually exclusive.
Yes; P(A and B) equals P(A)·P(B).
Yes; the two events cannot occur together.

items.prompt: In a group of 43, 29 do activity A, 16 do activity B, and 4 do both. Find P(A or B) as a fraction in lowest terms.

sections.title: Extension and challenge
sections.directions: Explain your method so that someone who has not done this unit could follow it.

items.prompt: An event has probability 3/11 on a single trial. Two independent trials are run. Find the probability of at least one success, as a fraction in lowest terms.
items.responseExpectation: Give the result and the reasoning that produced it. Show enough work that someone else could check each step.

items.prompt: A survey table records: group X with 36 successes and 24 failures; group Y with 17 successes and 34 failures. Find P(success | group X) as a fraction in lowest terms.
items.responseExpectation: Give the result and the reasoning that produced it. Show enough work that someone else could check each step.
